scenes.heading: Chemical kinetics
scenes.sub: Not whether it happens, but how fast
scenes.say: Thermodynamics tells you whether a reaction can happen. Kinetics tells you how fast, and by what pathway. It's why food lasts longer in the fridge, and how doctors decide how often you take a medicine.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Only athletes who clear the high-jump bar reach the other side
scenes.science: Only collisions with energy ≥ Eₐ and the right orientation react
scenes.breaks: a catalyst doesn't lower the same bar. It provides a whole new mechanism, and lowers the barrier for the reverse reaction too.
scenes.say: Activation energy is like a high-jump bar. Only collisions with enough energy and the right orientation get over it. Raising the temperature is like giving every athlete a better run-up, so many more clear the bar. A catalyst offers a different route with a lower bar.
scenes.caption: Activation energy, Eₐ, is like a high-jump bar. Only collisions with enough energy and the right orientation get over it. Raising the temperature is like a better run-up, so many more clear the bar. A catalyst offers a different route with a lower bar.

scenes.heading: Rate laws
points: Orders come from experiment, not the equation
Units of k change with overall order
scenes.say: A rate law says rate equals k times the concentrations raised to their orders. Those orders come from the lab, not the balanced equation. Double a concentration: if the rate stays the same, it's zero order. If it doubles, first order. If it quadruples, second order.

scenes.heading: Worked example: initial rates
scenes.question: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂. Doubling [NO] makes the rate ×4. Doubling [O₂] makes it ×2. Exp 1: 0.010 M each, rate 7.0 × 10⁻⁶ M s⁻¹.
scenes.say: Doubling nitric oxide quadruples the rate, so it's second order in N O. Doubling oxygen doubles the rate, so it's first order in oxygen. Substitute experiment one into the rate law, and k comes out at seven point zero per molar squared per second.
scenes.caption: Doubling [NO] quadruples the rate, so it's second order in NO. Doubling [O₂] doubles the rate, so it's first order in O₂. Substitute experiment 1, and k = 7.0 M⁻² s⁻¹.

scenes.heading: Zero, first and second order plots

right.title: Half-lives
points: First order: t½ = ln 2 ÷ k, constant
Zero order: each one gets shorter
Second order: each one gets longer

scenes.say: Zero is plain, first is natural log, second flips it. Those are the straight-line plots. First order is like popcorn popping. Every kernel has the same chance each second, so the half-life is always the same: natural log of two over k.
scenes.caption: Zero is plain, first is ln, second flips it. Those are the straight-line plots. First order is like popcorn popping. Every kernel has the same chance each second, so the half-life is always the same: t½ = ln 2 ÷ k.

scenes.heading: The Arrhenius equation
scenes.say: The Arrhenius equation shows how k depends on temperature. A plot of natural log k against one over T has a gradient of minus E a over R. If k doubles from twenty-five to thirty-five degrees, E a is fifty-two point nine kilojoules per mole.
scenes.caption: The Arrhenius equation shows how k depends on temperature. A plot of ln k against 1/T has a gradient of −Eₐ/R. If k doubles from 25.0 °C to 35.0 °C, Eₐ = 52.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

points: Orders come from the lab, not the equation
Only first order has a constant half-life
Slowest step sets the rate law
Catalysts lower Eₐ; ΔH and K unchanged
scenes.say: Quick recap. Orders come from experiment. Only first order has a steady half-life. The slowest step sets the pace, like the slowest checkpoint in a queue. And catalysts lower activation energy without changing delta H or K. Now try the practice questions!
